transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: James Park (Redwood AE), Sana Rao (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO - Aurelius), Marcus Chen (Platform Eng), Priya Sharma (SecOps)

Auto Summary (auto-generated): Discussed Private VPC deployment patterns, performance implications of KV-cache and batching across subnets, PrivateLink vs NAT egress, DNS resolution for internal endpoints, and quantization guidance for lower-cost instances. Action items captured.

Topics: PrivateLink, Transit Gateway, NAT egress, subnets (public/private), route tables, DNS resolution, KV cache locality, batching strategies, quantization/FP16 vs INT8, inference runtime kernel placement.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] James Park: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. I think we've got about 50 minutes so we'll try to cover networking patterns and then dig into the runtime implications yeah. Sana will run through the performance bits.
[00:18] Lena Ortiz: Thanks. We're really focused on understanding how Redwood will behave inside our VPC, and what network components we need to provision. We're trying to avoid unexpected egress costs and keep latency consistent for low-latency endpoints.
[00:28] Sana Rao: Great. I'll start with an overview of three patterns we typically see: PrivateLink endpoints into Redwood control plane + VPC endpoints for data plane, or a transit-managed model where you run the runtime inside your subnet with outbound NAT, or an on-prem air-gapped package. Each has tradeoffs.
[00:45] Marcus Chen: Quick clarifying q: when you say data plane do you mean the inference workers need to connect out to Redwood services or are they fully customer-hosted?
[00:55] James Park: Good question. In Private deployment, the inference runtime runs in your VPC (customer-owned), but optionally it calls back to Redwood control plane for billing, rollouts, metrics. You can use PrivateLink to keep those control-plane callbacks inside AWS' private network, so no public egress. If you want zero outbound at all, we do an on-prem bundle but that's a heavier install.
[01:12] Priya Sharma: And what about the store for KV cache, is that inside our VPC or do you host it? We care because of data residency and speed.
[01:22] Sana Rao: Important point. For Private VPC deployments the KV cache — we call it the KV cache or K V cache in docs — can be configured in two ways: local in-memory per-worker (lowest latency but limited size), or a shared cache service you host in your VPC (e.g., Redis/ElastiCache) that the workers connect to over internal network. We recommend colocated Redis in the same subnet or AZ to minimize cross-AZ latency; otherwise per-request latency for cache hits can jump.
[01:47] Marcus Chen: Colocated Redis — okay. If we do a shared cache across AZs are we going to see 3-5ms per token overhead? That's rough math but we'd like to quantify.
[01:58] Sana Rao: Yes, ballpark. For same-AZ within AZ local network it's sub-ms for a read; cross-AZ can be 2-6ms depending on instance types and peering. Also batching behavior matters: if you batch multiple requests into one GPU step you amortize KV lookup overhead.
[02:12] James Park: Right, batching is a big lever. For short-latency endpoints we often keep small batch sizes (e.g., 1-4) and rely on prefix KV cache hits to keep token latency low. For high throughput behind async queues, larger batch sizes (16-64) are used which changes where the latency is spent.
[02:28] Lena Ortiz: Can you explain how the runtime decides to hit the KV cache vs local cache? We saw some notes about continuous caching and prefix caching.
[02:36] Sana Rao: The runtime maintains per-worker KV cache for the current session. When a request arrives, we check per-worker local cache first; if there's no prefix match we consult the shared KV store if configured. There's also an adaptive strategy where the router can route repeat sessions to the same worker to maximize local KV hits — session affinity, or sticky routing. That needs sticky LB or our routing layer within the VPC.
[02:58] Marcus Chen: For sticky routing, does that require a stateful load balancer we run, like NLB with stickiness, or is that something Redwood provides as a sidecar?
[03:08] James Park: Redwood provides a lightweight routing component you can run as a DaemonSet; it uses consistent hashing to route sessions. Alternatively you can use NLB with source IP affinity, but we typically recommend the Redwood router for best KV locality.
[03:20] Priya Sharma: About PrivateLink: we need to know the DNS naming, certificates, and which AWS accounts to create endpoints in. Do you provide CloudFormation to provision these endpoints?
[03:30] James Park: We do. We'll send the CF/Terraform template. PrivateLink endpoints require an interface endpoint in your subnet and we create the service in our side — you'll need to accept the endpoint and we provide the service name and security group recommendations. DNS: we recommend you keep the private hosted zone and override the FQDN to point to the interface endpoint, that keeps everything inside the VPC.
[03:50] Lena Ortiz: If we use PrivateLink for control plane, does the data plane traffic (inference tokens and model weights) also flow through it? I want to avoid cross-account bandwidth or egress.
[03:59] Sana Rao: Typically model weights are pre-pulled and stored on the worker's local disk or EBS snapshot inside your VPC. Token-level traffic between your client and the runtime is internal. Control-plane calls (metrics, rollouts) go to Redwood via PrivateLink. If you choose a fully self-contained mode, no control-plane callbacks leave your VPC — that is the air-gapped / on-prem option.
[04:20] Marcus Chen: About DNS and mTLS: can we require mutual TLS between the router and Redwood control plane? Our SecOps mandates mTLS for all external services.
[04:28] James Park: Yes, we support mTLS for control-plane connections. For PrivateLink it can be optional because the interface endpoint keeps it private, but mTLS adds defense-in-depth. We'll provide cert rotation docs and recommend using your KMS for cert storage or integrate with ACM for certificates.
[04:46] Priya Sharma: KMS — do you integrate with customer-managed keys or do we use Redwood-managed? For compliance we need CMKs and audit logs.
[04:54] James Park: For Private deployments you can use your KMS for encryption at rest keys. We also produce audit logs and can ship to your CloudWatch / S3 bucket. We'll share the SOC2 + encryption docs in the security packet.
[05:05] Sana Rao: Back to performance: quantization changes latency vs accuracy. For many of Aurelius' LLM workloads with shorter contexts we see INT8 or 4-bit quantization reduces memory and can speed up inference by ~1.5-2x on certain runtimes, but kernel selection matters. Some kernels for FP16 are highly optimized on A100s and on T4/RTX certain INT8 paths are fast. We should test on the exact instance types you plan to run.
[05:32] Marcus Chen: We're looking at using G5s and some P4d. P4d has good FP16 perf, right?
[05:38] Sana Rao: P4d/P4de do well for FP16/FP32. For INT8 on GPUs you want to ensure the runtime picks quantized kernels; we've got profiles for G5, A100, H100 families. If you want cost-savings we can benchmark INT8 vs FP16 on your models.
[05:52] Lena Ortiz: About egress and NAT: we can't allow uncontrolled outbound to the internet, so how do we handle container image pulls and model pulls?
[06:00] James Park: Best practice: preseed images and model weights in a private ECR or S3 bucket accessible in your VPC. Use VPC endpoints for S3/ECR so you don't need NAT. If you need to pull from public registries, use an egress proxy or NAT with strict allowlist. We recommend using S3 VPC endpoints + ECR endpoints to avoid NAT charges.
[06:21] Priya Sharma: And route table stuff — are some subnets recommended to be public?
[06:25] Sana Rao: For the runtime workers themselves we recommend private subnets with no public IPs and access via a bastion or internal LB. For any interface endpoints (PrivateLink) you need interface endpoints in private subnets. If you plan to let certain admin hosts access the runtime from the internet, put them in a public subnet behind an ALB with WAF.
[06:44] Marcus Chen: One practical question: what about cross-account VPC peering vs PrivateLink? We have a hub-spoke topology with a transit gateway. Our security team likes TGW for centralized inspection.
[06:54] James Park: Transit Gateway works; you can route traffic to the Redwood worker subnets via TGW and keep central inspection. PrivateLink is useful when you want per-account interface endpoints and a simple DNS mapping. TGW gives you centralized routing but you must manage route propagation and ensure low-latency paths between spoke and worker AZs. For KV cache locality, avoid spanning AZs unnecessarily.
[07:14] Lena Ortiz: We're trying to hit under 150ms tail latency for a 256-token prompt with streaming enabled. Any concerns?
[07:23] Sana Rao: 150ms is tight but achievable with right sizing: smaller batch sizes, colocated KV cache, local model weights on NVMe, and use of optimized kernels (FP16 on P4/A100). Also watch network jitter from cross-AZ calls and ensure your VPC's ENI attachment limits aren't throttling throughput.
[07:39] Marcus Chen: ENI limits — good call. We'll check our accounts. Also curious — does Redwood runtime support kernel-level optimizations like flash attention and fused kernels?
[07:47] Sana Rao: Yes, our runtime picks tuned kernels, yes flash attention, fused MLPs where beneficial. We have a compilation phase that selects kernels based on model size and seq length distribution. We'll include the runtime profile that shows recommended instance families for your model.
[08:05] Priya Sharma: A couple security items: does the runtime create any IAM roles that allow cross-account writes? Our policy restricts broad role permissions.
[08:12] James Park: The deployed agents need scoped IAM for S3/ECR access and for CloudWatch logs if you enable it. We provide minimal policy templates - least privilege - and avoid wide STS permissions. We'll send examples.
[08:22] Lena Ortiz: If we run benchmarks in our VPC, what's the recommended test harness to simulate client traffic and measure tail latency?
[08:29] Sana Rao: We provide a lightweight load runner that simulates concurrent sessions with configurable seq lengths and token delays to exercise KV cache patterns. It emits p99/p95/p50 and per-token timing. We'll run it with you — Sana: (to-do) attach the harness to an isolated subnet and we'll capture metrics.
[08:45] Marcus Chen: Any gotchas with DNS TTLs for failover between AZs when using PrivateLink?
[08:51] James Park: DNS TTLs on interface endpoints are typically low; but if you use a private hosted zone and alias record to the endpoint, during failover there might be a brief resolution mismatch. We recommend health checks and our client retry logic with exponential backoff to handle transient DNS flaps.
[09:07] Priya Sharma: Can we get logs shipped to our SIEM for model inference audit trails? We need to see who called what and when for compliance.
[09:14] James Park: Yes, audit logs can be exported to CloudWatch or S3 and then forwarded to your SIEM. We can include token-level metadata (not content) to preserve PII policies; content logging is opt-in and should be gated.
[09:29] Lena Ortiz: You mentioned model pre-pull. How do you handle model updates and rollouts without causing disk thrash — we have limited NVMe.
[09:37] Sana Rao: We do staged rollouts: prefetch model artifacts to a warm directory and use atomic symlink swaps to flip the active model. You can configure max concurrent model downloads per host. Also set eviction policies for least-recently used models.
[09:52] Marcus Chen: What's the memory footprint with 8-bit quant vs FP16 for our 13B model?
[09:58] Sana Rao: 13B: FP16 roughly ~26GB parameter memory + activations; 8-bit quant reduces parameter store to ~13GB but activations still consume similar space. So you might fit more models per GPU with quantization, but activations limit throughput for long contexts.
[10:17] Lena Ortiz: For the benchmark run can we test multiple instance types and quantization configs?
[10:21] Sana Rao: Absolutely, we'll collect perf numbers across G5, A100, and P4d with FP16 and INT8. We'll include per-token cost estimates.
[10:29] James Park: Quick recap and next steps — we'll share the PrivateLink + TF templates, CF templates, the runtime profile and the load-harness. Sana will run a benchmark plan with you and we will schedule the security deep-dive with Priya. Anything else from the Aurelius side?
[10:41] Priya Sharma: Please include guidance for certificate lifecycle and KMS integration. Also send the minimal IAM policy.
[10:48] James Park: Will do.
[10:50] Lena Ortiz: Thanks, that was helpful. We'll review and pick preferred instance families; Marcus will coordinate the benchmark infra.
[10:58] James Park: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and proposed times for the security review.
